presidents.name: Herbert Hoover
presidents.summary: Hoover nominated federal appeals judge John J. Parker to the Supreme Court in 1930, and the NAACP ran a public campaign against him over a 1920 statement opposing Black participation in politics; the Senate rejected Parker on May 7, 1930. His administration also ran the government-funded Gold Star Mothers pilgrimages to France on a racially separated basis beginning in 1930.
presidents.paragraph: Hoover's best-documented dealings with Black Americans mostly went badly for them. On March 21, 1930 he sent John J. Parker's name to the Senate for the Supreme Court. Parker, running for governor of North Carolina in 1920, had called Black political participation "a source of evil and danger to both races." The NAACP ran what the Library of Congress calls its first successful campaign against a Supreme Court nominee, organized labor joined over Parker's anti-union ruling, and the Senate voted him down 41 to 39 on May 7, 1930. That same year Hoover's War Department began sending Gold Star mothers and widows to visit their sons' graves in France, and split the travelers by race; the administration said the separation was "in the interests of the pilgrims themselves." Of roughly 1,593 eligible Black mothers and widows, only 233 accepted and fewer than 200 sailed. Earlier, as Coolidge's flood coordinator in 1927, Hoover oversaw relief camps where Black refugees were held under guard, and he appointed Robert Moton's Colored Advisory Commission, which documented the abuses.

presidents.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
presidents.summary: Roosevelt signed Executive Order 8802 on June 25, 1941, barring racial discrimination in defense industries and federal employment and creating the Fair Employment Practice Committee, after A. Philip Randolph threatened a mass march on Washington. He did not publicly back federal anti-lynching legislation, and the Social Security Act he signed in 1935 excluded agricultural and domestic workers, categories that covered most employed Black Americans.
presidents.paragraph: Roosevelt's record here is two things at once. In 1941 A. Philip Randolph and other Black leaders told the administration they were ready to bring tens of thousands of people to Washington unless job discrimination in war plants ended. On June 25, 1941 Roosevelt signed Executive Order 8802, which said there'd be "no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries or government because of race, creed, color, or national origin," and set up the Fair Employment Practice Committee to take complaints. The march was called off. But when the Costigan-Wagner anti-lynching bill hit a southern filibuster in 1935, Roosevelt stayed quiet; he needed those same southern Democrats for the New Deal, and the bill died without a vote. The Social Security Act he signed that August left out agricultural and domestic workers, and at least 60 percent of the Black population worked in those categories. He also promoted Benjamin O. Davis Sr., the first Black general officer in the U.S. armed forces.

disputes: Whether the Social Security Act's agricultural and domestic exclusions were racially motivated is actively contested. SSA's own Social Security Bulletin summarizes the view that the Roosevelt administration 'acceded to a Southern amendment' to satisfy southern congressmen, and then argues the racial-bias thesis is 'conceptually flawed and unsupported by the existing empirical evidence,' pointing instead to administrative collection difficulties. Both positions are recorded here without resolution.

The date of Benjamin O. Davis Sr.'s promotion: the Army Center of Military History records a temporary brigadier-general promotion on October 25, 1940 and a regular-Army promotion on August 1, 1941, and different official pages lead with different dates.

presidents.name: Harry S. Truman
presidents.summary: Truman created the President's Committee on Civil Rights by Executive Order 9808 on December 5, 1946, and its 1947 report To Secure These Rights documented discrimination in voting, housing, education and public accommodations. On July 26, 1948 he signed Executive Order 9981, requiring equality of treatment and opportunity in the armed forces, and Executive Order 9980, barring discrimination in federal employment.
presidents.paragraph: Truman moved on civil rights mainly through executive power, because Congress wouldn't move. After the 1946 beating and blinding of Sgt. Isaac Woodard, a decorated Black veteran pulled off a bus in South Carolina, Truman issued Executive Order 9808 on December 5, 1946 creating the President's Committee on Civil Rights. Its 1947 report, To Secure These Rights, laid out discrimination in voting, housing, education and public accommodations. On February 2, 1948 he asked a joint session of Congress for federal anti-lynching protection, voting rights safeguards and a permanent Fair Employment Practices Commission. Congress didn't deliver, so on July 26, 1948 he signed two orders: 9981, requiring "equality of treatment and opportunity for all persons in the armed forces," and 9980, directing that federal personnel actions be based "solely on merit and fitness" with no discrimination by race, color, religion or national origin. He was also the first president to address the NAACP, speaking at the Lincoln Memorial on June 29, 1947.

presidents.personalRecord: Truman's own private and public language conflicted with his official record. In a June 22, 1911 letter to Bess Wallace, published by the Truman Library, he wrote that one man is as good as another "so long as he's honest and decent and not a nigger or a Chinaman," and added that he was "strongly of the opinion that negroes ought to be in Africa." As a senator, addressing the National Colored Democratic Association in Chicago on July 14, 1940, he said: "I wish to make it clear that I am not appealing for social equality of the Negro... Negroes want justice, not social relations."

disputes: Motive behind EO 9981 is contested. The Truman Library frames the question itself — 'Idealistic, Pragmatic, or Shrewd Politician?' — placing his 1911 and 1940 statements alongside the 1948 orders; other accounts, including the National Park Service, emphasize the political cost he paid as the Democratic Party split before the 1948 election.

How far EO 9981 went in practice is described differently: the National Park Service calls it 'ending military segregation,' while the order's own text commits only to equality of treatment and opportunity 'as rapidly as possible,' with implementation running for years afterward.
unverified: The exact release date of To Secure These Rights (commonly given as October 29, 1947) — the Truman Library page returned unreadable content and no fetched source stated the day.
Whether the Justice Department's prosecution of the officer who blinded Isaac Woodard ended in acquittal — the outcome was not stated in the fetched text.

presidents.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
presidents.summary: Eisenhower signed Executive Order 10730 on September 24, 1957 and sent the 101st Airborne Division to Little Rock, Arkansas, to enforce a federal court desegregation order at Central High School. He signed the Civil Rights Act of 1957 (P.L. 85-315) on September 9, 1957 and the Civil Rights Act of 1960 (P.L. 86-449) on May 6, 1960, and never publicly endorsed the Brown v. Board of Education decision.
presidents.paragraph: Eisenhower did the enforcing without doing the endorsing. When Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock's Central High School, Eisenhower signed Executive Order 10730 on September 24, 1957, authorizing the Secretary of Defense to use "such of the armed forces of the United States as he may deem necessary," and ordered the 101st Airborne in. He'd already signed the Civil Rights Act of 1957 on September 9 at Newport, Rhode Island: the first civil rights legislation since Reconstruction, creating a Civil Rights Commission and a Civil Rights Division at Justice, though Congress had stripped out the stronger voting protections. The 1960 act, signed May 6, added federal voting referees and record-retention requirements. On Brown itself he stayed carefully neutral, saying the Court had spoken and he was sworn to obey, and earlier that he did not believe "we can cure all the evils in men's hearts by law."

disputes: Assessments of Eisenhower's overall civil rights leadership diverge. The National Park Service, citing historian William Hitchcock, describes an administration that 'marked a turning point in the Civil Rights movement' while his personal leadership stayed hesitant; the Miller Center emphasizes that he 'did not champion the need for equality and fairness' and did not embrace Brown.

Whether Eisenhower's Little Rock intervention reflected support for desegregation or only for federal court authority: the Eisenhower Library frames it as enforcing the Supreme Court's ruling, while the National Park Service notes he acted only after 'initial reluctance' and once a federal injunction gave him clear authority.
unverified: The frequently repeated account of Eisenhower telling Chief Justice Earl Warren at a 1954 White House dinner that southern segregationists were not bad people — anecdotal and not verified from any source fetched here.
Specific claims about desegregation of Washington, D.C. public facilities and Navy yards under Eisenhower — mentioned in passing but not documented in the text fetched.
